title: What are tendons and tendon sheaths?
intro: Tendons are strong cords of fibrous tissue that connect muscles to bones and transmit the force that moves the body. Many tendons are surrounded by tendon sheaths, which allow them to glide smoothly. Tendon problems are common in people who do repetitive or heavy activities and in sport.

sections.heading: Structure and function
paragraphs: Tendons consist mainly of tightly packed collagen fibres, which make them very strong yet slightly flexible. When a muscle contracts, the tendon pulls on the bone and moves the joint. The Achilles tendon, which connects the calf muscles to the heel, is the thickest and strongest in the body. Tendons store and release elastic energy, helping with walking and running.

sections.heading: Tendon sheaths
paragraphs: In places where tendons pass under ligaments or around corners, such as the wrist, hand, fingers and ankle, they run in sheaths lined with a thin membrane that produces a lubricating fluid. This reduces friction. Inflammation of the sheath is called tenosynovitis. Bursae, small fluid-filled sacs near joints, also reduce friction.

sections.heading: Common problems
paragraphs: Tendinopathy is overuse injury with pain and thickening of the tendon, for example in the Achilles tendon, the elbow and the shoulder. Tendon sheath inflammation causes pain and swelling and in the fingers can cause trigger finger. Partial or complete ruptures can occur from sudden load or degeneration, and may cause a snapping sensation and loss of function.

sections.heading: Healing
paragraphs: Tendons have a limited blood supply, so they heal slowly. Treatment usually includes activity changes, progressive strengthening exercises and sometimes injections or surgery. Complete ruptures of some tendons, such as the Achilles, may need surgery or specialised splinting. Rehabilitation takes months.

sections.heading: Looking after tendons
paragraphs: Warm up before exercise, increase training gradually, include strength training, use suitable equipment and allow time for recovery. Some medicines, such as certain antibiotics from the quinolone group, and corticosteroids, can increase the risk of tendon problems. Report sudden tendon pain, particularly when taking these medicines.

examples.title: Warming up
examples.text: Imagine you start running again after a break. You could begin with short, slow runs, add a gentle warm-up and increase distance by small steps.

examples.title: Reporting pain
examples.text: Suppose you take an antibiotic and notice pain in your Achilles tendon. You might stop activity and call your doctor promptly.
